I have farmed these 4.1 mu for half a century. I know every patch of soil. My son and his wife work in a factory in town, so they send money home, but I am the one who decides what happens on this land. I am 70 now—my back is not strong like before—so I hire the tractor driver for tillage and sowing, but I still make all the decisions myself.

This year, I will keep doing what has always worked: wheat-maize double cropping on the full 4.1 mu. I cannot afford to leave land idle, and we need both crops for food and cash.

For **wheat**, I will sow Jimai 22 in autumn—it is the improved variety that has done well here for years, and I trust it. Before sowing, I will have the tractor do rotary tillage to break up the stubble and make a fine seedbed. I will apply about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, mostly from compound fertilizer—some as basal and the rest topdressed at green-up. Too much nitrogen makes the wheat lodge, and at my age I cannot afford that risk. I will irrigate three times: once at sowing if the autumn is dry, once at jointing in spring, and once at grain filling. The well water is reliable, but pumping costs electricity, so I do not waste it. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide once or twice if I see aphids or disease. If the weather is normal, I expect about 480 kg per mu.

For **maize**, as soon as the wheat comes off the field in early June—usually around June 8th or 10th—I will plant Deng Hai 605 hybrid seed. The window is short, so I use the no-tillage seeder that plants directly into the wheat stubble. It saves time, labor, and fuel. I will apply about 13 kg of nitrogen per mu, less than wheat, because maize does not need as much. I will irrigate twice: once right after sowing if it does not rain within two days, and once at the big trumpet stage. If the summer rains are good, maybe I can get by with just one irrigation, but I will keep two in my plan to be safe. I will spray for weeds and insects two or three times. I expect about 520 kg per mu.

That is my plan. I do not chase new fashions. I do what the land and my experience tell me to do.
